title: BlueHarbor Labs - p95 / concurrency / streaming discovery
summary: Intro discovery focused on p95 latency targets for streaming responses, concurrency requirements for interactive agents, and token/sec benchmarking. Redwood AE + SE covered hosted vs dedicated vs private tradeoffs, batching & KV cache impacts, and proposed a joint benchmark plan + pricing follow-up.
next_steps: Redwood: send detailed benchmark plan & synthetic workload script (by 2025-11-24)
BlueHarbor: share representative prompt set + expected user concurrency windows (by 2025-11-25)
Schedule 1-hour pilot run (load test) with BlueHarbor datasets (week of 2025-12-01)
Redwood: provide Dedicated capacity pricing options and edge-region latency estimates (by 2025-11-27)
action_items: Sasha: attach pricing sheet + Dedicated capacity tiers; due 2025-11-27
Ravi: prepare synthetic benchmark script and run a baseline on hosted; due 2025-11-24
Ethan: upload 50 representative prompts and 3 streaming examples to the shared S3 link; due 2025-11-25
Priya: confirm expected concurrency distribution (10/100/1000 users) and VPC constraints; due 2025-11-25
transcript:
Header: 2025-11-20 15:00 UTC | Duration: 57m | Recording id: ff-20251120-0037
Attendees: Sasha Patel (Redwood AE), Ravi Menon (Redwood SE), Maria Gomez (BlueHarbor CTO), Ethan Li (ML Eng), Priya Singh (Platform Eng)

[00:00:00] Sasha: Hi everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Sasha, AE at Redwood - joining with Ravi from our SE team. Quick round robin?
[00:00:12] Maria: Hi, Maria here. CTO at BlueHarbor. We build AI-driven search assistants for maritime logistics — latency is huge for us.
[00:00:20] Ethan: Ethan, ML Eng, mostly running model infra and benchmarks.
[00:00:24] Priya: Priya, platform eng, handles VPC and on-prem network for us.
[00:00:29] Sasha: Great. Goal for today: understand your p95 targets, concurrency profile, and whether Hosted/Dedicated/Private makes sense. We'll also talk token/sec expectations and propose a benchmarking plan.
[00:00:45] Ravi: Quick caveat, transcription might mangle some acronyms — K V cache sometimes comes out as K-V cash in our notes, sorry in advance.
[00:00:52] Maria: haha okay. To start, our product surface is real-time chat with step-by-step guidance. Target p95 per-user latency for a streaming answer is sub-350ms for short replies (<=150 tokens) and sub-900ms for longer shoulder-length responses (~400 tokens). Those are ambitious but key for our UX.
[00:01:14] Sasha: Good, that's helpful. When you say streaming, do you require incremental token-by-token streaming (SSE / chunked) or batched chunked responses is fine?
[00:01:24] Maria: Prefer token streaming for perceived latency, but we can tolerate small batching if it buys throughput.
[00:01:31] Ethan: Also important: concurrency. Our daily peak is about 350 concurrent active users, but peak windows see up to 900 concurrent during certain schedules. Average session length is 2.3 minutes, median reply size ~120 tokens.
[00:01:45] Priya: And network constraint: some customers route via private VPC peering, others via public internet. For compliance we need audit logs and KMS integration in the dedicated/private option.
[00:01:58] Ravi: Understood. A couple things to call out — p95 is very sensitive to batching and KV cache hit rates. If you have a high prefix reuse, KV caching can bring token/sec up and p95 down. But for conversation heavy flows with fresh contexts, you see lower cache hit and higher variance.
[00:02:20] Sasha: For Hosted we normally publish our observed p95 baselines for our curated model set — for a 7B-ish open model on standard infra we typically hit p95 streaming of ~120-220ms per token under light concurrency, but end-to-end user-perceived p95 for 150-token replies will be higher because of generation time across tokens.
[00:02:40] Maria: Can you give an expected p95 for full reply 150 tokens — not per token — like end-to-end from request to last token?
[00:02:49] Ravi: Rough ballpark: if you stream tokens as they generate and your UI considers first meaningful token as the key metric, you can see first-token p95 <200ms and last-token p95 depend on tokens/sec; at 50 tokens/sec you'd finish 150 tokens in ~3s so p95 ~3s. If you need total reply under 900ms for 400 tokens, you'd need >400 tokens/sec which implies aggressive batching and larger GPUs or a streaming-optimized model.
[00:03:16] Ethan: 400 tokens in <900ms seems unrealistic unless running high-end GPU and shorter context, right?
[00:03:22] Ravi: Correct — that's an extreme. Two levers: model architecture/quantization and hardware. Dedicated pools with multi-GPU or faster A100/L40 can drive higher tokens/sec. Also Redwood Optimize suggestions (quantization + kernel choices) can boost throughput.
[00:03:38] Maria: Our UX team cares about time-to-first-meaningful-token more than final token; so maybe we prioritize first token p95 and steady streaming throughput.
[00:03:46] Sasha: Noted. Can you share your SLOs in order (p95 first-token, p95 end-to-end, 99th)?
[00:03:54] Maria: Sure: First-token p95 <=200ms; end-to-end for typical 150-token reply p95 <=2.5s; end-to-end for long replies (300–400 tokens) p95 <=6s; concurrency scaling to 1k sustained for short bursts.
[00:04:09] Priya: On compliance, SOC2 + KMS + SSO (SAML) is mandatory for Dedicated or Private. For Hosted, we need contractual guarantees on data retention and per-customer logs.
[00:04:21] Sasha: We'll include our SOC2 pack and KMS integration guide. For Hosted we can enable per-customer tenancy with retention policies, but Dedicated gives stronger isolation and predictable tail-latency under heavy load.
[00:04:34] [00:04:40] Ethan: How should we think about concurrency vs batching? If we need 900 concurrent sessions, do you recommend Dedicated?
[00:04:47] Ravi: Generally, Dedicated simplifies capacity planning for sustained high concurrency. With hosted, you can hit cold-scaling or noisy neighbor effects at extreme spikes. We can route by policy to fallback models too. For 900 sustained concurrent interactive sessions with sub-second first-token p95, Dedicated or Private is likely the right path.
[00:05:05] Maria: Pricing is also a factor — Dedicated is more expensive but predictable. We need ballpark numbers.
[00:05:11] Sasha: We'll send tiered Dedicated pricing and an estimated token cost delta vs Hosted. We'll also provide a cost projection for a 900-concurrency steady workload.
[00:05:19] [00:05:40] Priya: On networking for Private: we need to know if Redwood supports customer-managed KMS/HSM and if audit logs can be forwarded to our SIEM.
[00:05:48] Ravi: Yes. Private supports KMS integration and HSM in our on-prem package; audit logging can be shipped to your SIEM. We'll include a tech note.
[00:05:57] Maria: For benchmarks, we want realistic token/sec numbers. What do you usually see per GPU for streaming for 7B vs 13B vs 70B models? Also how much does quantization shift numbers?
[00:06:12] Ravi: Rough public numbers (very approximate): 7B quantized low-precision on an A10-ish host: 100-300 tokens/sec; 13B on an A10 maybe 40-120 tokens/sec; 70B on A100 or L40 could be 200-800 tokens/sec depending on kernel and quantization. Quantization (int8/4) can often give 1.5x-3x throughput gains but can affect output quality. We'll include model-specific perf profiles.
[00:06:41] Ethan: Do you run continuous batching or prefer synchronous streaming?
[00:06:45] Ravi: Redwood supports continuous batching with preservation of streaming semantics (we call it continuous token streaming). It tries to batch similar-length requests to maximize GPU utilization without violating latency SLOs. You can tune max batch size and latency budget.
[00:06:58] Maria: Any suggestions on how to structure prompts to improve cache hits?
[00:07:03] Ravi: Prefixing common system instructions and separating volatile user content can help. We'll share a prompt engineering note — but KV cache hits come from shared prefixes. If you see many identical conversation turns or templates, caching helps a lot.
[00:07:16] [00:07:40] Ethan: Can Redwood run a quick sanity test on our sample prompts? Like run hosted baseline and report p95?
[00:07:47] Sasha: Yes — that's part of the benchmark plan. We'll ask you to upload representative prompts and a short data sample; then Ravi will run a hosted baseline and report numbers. If numbers look close, we can propose a Dedicated pool spec for predictable tails.
[00:07:59] Priya: For the pilot load test, what's the typical cadence? How many hours and what ramp?
[00:08:05] Ravi: For a valid pilot: 2–4 hours with steady-state at target concurrency and a 20–30 minute ramp up/down. We'll also run a 15–30 minute spike test to observe tail behavior. We'll capture token/sec, p50/p95/p99, and KV cache hit rates.
[00:08:22] Maria: Good. Also curious about streaming over mobile networks — do you have any edge optimizations or regional routing?
[00:08:29] Sasha: We can route requests to nearest region. For very latency-sensitive use cases, we recommend Dedicated pools in the target region. We also expose route policy so you can prefer low-latency regions and fallback to lower-cost regions on overload.
[00:08:41] [00:09:10] Ethan: About measuring perceived latency: should we prioritize time-to-first-byte or first-meaningful-token? We think the latter is more aligned with UX.
[00:09:18] Ravi: Agree — first-meaningful-token is better. Our benchmark script will capture both TTFB, first-token, and last-token times so you can correlate.
[00:09:28] Maria: Any red flags we should watch for in our prompt set? Long contexts >8k will blow up memory and impact throughput, correct?
[00:09:36] Ravi: Yes. Long contexts raise KV size and memory pressure. If you have long history, we recommend summarization or rolling context windows and agressive KV caching for reused prefixes.
[00:09:49] Priya: For security docs, please send SOC2, encryption in transit and at rest, data retention policy and audit log export examples.
[00:09:58] Sasha: Will do. We'll attach our security pack in the follow-up.
[00:10:05] [00:10:30] Maria: Let's talk about real numbers we'd accept: p95 first-token <=200ms, and p95 end-to-end for 150-token replies <=2.5s. If you can't meet that on Hosted, then Dedicated or Private is required. Can you commit to a benchmark that proves it?
[00:10:45] Ravi: We can run that. We'll configure a hosted baseline with your prompt set; if we see tail issues we can propose Dedicated pool sizing (GPU type + instances) and estimate tokens/sec to meet your SLOs. We'll also simulate network variance.
[00:11:00] Ethan: When you size Dedicated, do you give an estimate in terms of GPUs or qps?
[00:11:06] Ravi: We give both. Example: to hit sustained 900 concurrent short sessions with first-token p95 <=200ms, you might need X number of A100 equivalents or Y L40s depending on model. We'll produce a costed scenario.
[00:11:18] Maria: Any pitfalls with video/audio multimodal contexts? We may start streaming a small transcription with video soon.
[00:11:25] Ravi: Multimodal increases preproc time but serving is similar. If transcriptions are long, treat them as context and consider summarization pre-step to reduce token counts.
[00:11:36] [00:11:55] Sasha: Quick recap of next actions: we'll send benchmark plan, security docs, pricing options and schedule pilot run. BlueHarbor will share prompt set and concurrency profile.
[00:12:05] Maria: Sounds good. One last quick question: can Redwood do enforced session affinity for KV caching? We want conversation sticky to the same worker for cache benefits.
[00:12:15] Ravi: We support affinity policies; for Dedicated it's straightforward, for Hosted we can provide affinity tokens but we still maintain autoscaling. We'll document the exact guarantees.
[00:12:27] Priya: Great. Also, can you include an example of how fallback routing works if a Dedicated pool is saturated?
[00:12:34] Sasha: Yes — typical fallback is to a lower-capacity model or to a different region; we'll include a flow diagram.
[00:12:42] [00:13:00] Ethan: Thank you. Look forward to numbers.
[00:13:03] Maria: Thanks everyone.
[00:56:40] Sasha: wrapping up — will follow up with the attachments and proposed dates for pilot.
[00:56:55] Meeting ended.

Notes: occasional transcription errors present ("K V cash" for KV cache, "samel" for SAML). Shared artifacts referenced: security pack (link: internal redwood-sec-pack.pdf), pricing deck (link: redwood-dedicated-pricing.xlsx), benchmark script repo (link: github.com/redwood/bench-script)
